Opening

GROW · SCIENCE · Autumn 2 · Week 3 · LESSON A · 2 MINUTES

Solar System Research: Evidence Desk

Learning objective

I can check a focused solar-system question using named sources and present three accurate facts in my own words.

Success looks like

  • Select relevant facts and retain their source codes.
  • Compare a claim across two named organisations.
  • Present three facts with units, a source and an honest limit.

Your mission is to prepare a short briefing someone else can trust. The nine supplied source cards allow a complete offline route.

Two separate lessons

A · Explore and explain · 40 minutes

B · Solar System Presentation: Mission Briefing · 40 minutes

Stop after Lesson A. Lesson B has its own start and exit.

Point, speak, sign, move cards, draw, write or direct an adult. Choose one route; equivalent science evidence does not require a written conversion.

Watch, predict, explain

Predict, model, explain

My claim is ___. Source ___ says ___. Source ___ agrees / adds detail / needs checking.

Make a prediction. Change one view, then use a label to explain what you notice.

Ask one focused question about Saturn’s rings, Mars’s colour or Jupiter’s rotation.

Worked explanation · reveal after thinking

Source cards are new paraphrases of the named NASA and ESA pages, checked 16 September 2026. No current moon counts are used. NASA “about 10 hours” and ESA 9.93 hours for Jupiter agree at different rounding levels. Mars’s reddish dust contains iron oxides; recent mineral interpretations must not be presented as certainty about life.

Local explainer · 32 seconds · silent with captions

Use instead of part of the demonstration. It never autoplays and needs no internet.

Full text / no-video alternative

00–08 seconds · Choose a question
Ask one focused question about Saturn’s rings, Mars’s colour or Jupiter’s rotation.

08–16 seconds · Check a source
Keep the organisation, source code and units beside the fact. Do not copy an anonymous claim.

16–24 seconds · Compare meaning
About 10 hours and 9.93 hours describe nearly the same rotation period, with different rounding.

24–32 seconds · Brief an audience
Use three checked facts in your own words, visible source codes and one honest limit.

Read the card clues

Named rings source: SAT-A links “mainly ice particles” to NASA’s Saturn facts.

Unit retained: JUP-A says about 10 hours for one rotation.

Unsourced life claim: “Red dust proves animals live on Mars” is not supported by these cards.

Old copied note: An undated note gives no source or unit; locate the original before using it.

Two rotation values: 9.93 hours and about 10 hours agree after rounding.

Solid ring claim: The supplied sources describe particles, not one solid ring.

Supplied resources · read or print

Source bank · Saturn’s rings

Question

What are Saturn’s rings like? These are paraphrased source cards, not direct quotations.

SAT-A · NASA Saturn facts

Saturn’s rings are made mainly of pieces of ice, with rock and dust also present. Own-word note: mainly ice particles.

SAT-B · ESA Saturn’s rings

The rings contain separate fragments of ice and rock; they are not one solid sheet. Compare the material claim with SAT-A.

SAT-C · NASA Saturn facts

Ring particles vary greatly in size. A smooth-looking ring in a small picture does not mean a continuous solid surface.

Check

Find one claim shared by NASA and ESA. Keep all source codes; the Teacher Pack lists the exact pages.

Source bank · Mars’s colour

Question

Why does Mars look reddish? These cards summarise sources, not measurements by this class.

MAR-A · NASA Mars facts

Iron minerals in surface material have oxidised. Iron oxides contribute to the reddish dust.

MAR-B · ESA Mars Express

Research reported in 2025 found that a water-containing iron mineral, ferrihydrite, gives a good match to the dust’s colour. The broad iron-oxide explanation agrees with MAR-A; this adds detail.

MAR-C · NASA Mars facts

Mars’s surface is not uniformly red: other colours occur. A distant reddish appearance does not describe every rock or place.

Check

Do not turn mineral evidence into proof of life, or colour into a temperature measurement. The exact source pages are in the Teacher Pack.

Source bank · Jupiter’s day

Question

How long is Jupiter’s day, and how is it different from its year?

JUP-A · NASA Jupiter facts

Jupiter completes a rotation in about 10 hours. A day here refers to the planet’s rotation.

JUP-B · ESA Juice facts

ESA gives a day length of 9.93 hours. Rounded to a whole hour, this agrees with about 10 hours.

JUP-C · NASA Jupiter facts

Jupiter takes about 12 Earth years to orbit the Sun. A year refers to an orbit, not a rotation.

Check

Keep hours and Earth years distinct. Different rounded values need not conflict. The exact source pages are in the Teacher Pack.

You do

GROW · SCIENCE · Autumn 2 · Week 3 · LESSON A · 10 MINUTES

Use the evidence yourself

Supported · use one response mode

1. Choose and collect

Choose one question. Select three relevant source-bank facts with an adult.

Help: Use one complete three-card question set.

2. Check one claim

Match one NASA fact to an agreeing ESA card.

Help: Choose the paired source codes.

3. Prepare to present

Place your three facts in a clear order.

Help: Point to a title and three fact spaces.

Standard · use one response mode

1. Choose and collect

Choose a question and record three relevant facts in your own words.

Help: Keep each source code.

2. Check one claim

Compare one claim across two named organisations.

Help: Compare meanings, not identical wording.

3. Prepare to present

Plan a question, three facts and a sources line.

Help: Use the supplied storyboard.

Stretch · use one response mode

1. Choose and collect

Select three precise facts, retaining units and any uncertainty.

Help: Reject interesting but irrelevant facts.

2. Check one claim

Explain agreement, extra detail or a remaining uncertainty; do not invent a contradiction.

Help: Consider rounding and shared research.

3. Prepare to present

Add a precise limitation and a checkable explanation for a non-expert audience.

Help: Distinguish observation from speculation.

Use the application model · an alternative to writing

Check the briefing decisions

Use the digital choices or the matching paper page. One response mode is enough.

Workshop

GROW · SCIENCE · Autumn 2 · Week 3 · LESSON B · 20 MINUTES

Gather and use evidence

Use the supplied offline source bank. Optional web checking is adult-supervised with no logins or pupil personal data. Pupils may point to source codes, dictate, type or use the paper storyboard; a public spoken performance is not compulsory.

4 min · Recheck a source, unit and question.
20 min · Build a one-page or three-slide briefing from the source bank. Rehearse with a partner, adult or typed explanation.
2 min · Listener checks one fact against its source card.
6 min · Keep the first version and improve one scientific detail.
Briefing partWhat the audience needs
QuestionOne focused question
Facts 1–3Three relevant facts in your own words
CheckTwo source codes and what agrees
LimitOne thing the evidence does not establish

Supported route

Use the four-part storyboard. Select three fact strips and point to two source codes; an adult can read your explanation to one listener.

Standard route

Present three relevant facts with sources and an agreement check. Record one audience question and improve the science detail.

Stretch route

Explain approximation or uncertainty, discuss whether sources share evidence, and answer a listener’s question without adding an unsupported claim.

Check the briefing decisions

Use the digital choices or the matching paper page. One response mode is enough.

Check

GROW · SCIENCE · Autumn 2 · Week 3 · LESSON B · 2 MINUTES

Check one piece of evidence

Check one piece of evidence

Can a listener find the source of one fact? Does every number have a unit, and does “about” remain where needed?

Worked explanation · reveal after thinking

Accept any accurate three-fact briefing based on the supplied bank. Example Jupiter: one rotation is about 10 hours (JUP-A); ESA reports 9.93 hours (JUP-B); one orbit takes about 12 Earth years (JUP-C). The first two agree by rounding. Day and year measure different motions. This does not establish an exact period at every atmospheric latitude.

Knowledge organiser

GROW Science · Autumn 2 · Week 3 · Shared resource · Shared resource

Learning objective

I can check a focused solar-system question using named sources and present three accurate facts in my own words.

Key words

source — where information came from

claim — something that can be checked

corroborate — check whether another source agrees

approximate — rounded, not exact

paraphrase — explain an idea in your own words

Remember

  • Choose a question before collecting facts.
  • Keep units and words such as about.
  • Check the actual source, not only its logo.
  • Two pages can repeat one study; agreement is useful but is not independent proof.

Success looks like

  • Select relevant facts and retain their source codes.
  • Compare a claim across two named organisations.
  • Present three facts with units, a source and an honest limit.

My claim is ___. Source ___ says ___. Source ___ agrees / adds detail / needs checking.

source
where information came from

something that can be checked

TA Brief

Current stage

Current stage:

Preparation and access

Use the supplied offline source bank. Optional web checking is adult-supervised with no logins or pupil personal data. Pupils may point to source codes, dictate, type or use the paper storyboard; a public spoken performance is not compulsory.

Scientific care

Source cards are new paraphrases of the named NASA and ESA pages, checked 16 September 2026. No current moon counts are used. NASA “about 10 hours” and ESA 9.93 hours for Jupiter agree at different rounding levels. Mars’s reddish dust contains iron oxides; recent mineral interpretations must not be presented as certainty about life.

Responsive feedback within teaching

The lesson teacher hears an optional request, explains what can change, tries it and checks the effect. Passing or asking privately is valid. No compulsory participation task or new pupil form. Do not infer assessment codes from a click, download or written box.

Sources and scope

  • NASA · Saturn facts
  • ESA · Saturn’s rings
  • NASA · Mars facts
  • ESA · Why Mars is red: updated evidence
  • NASA · Jupiter facts
  • ESA · Facts about Jupiter
  • Original lesson A
  • Original lesson B

Arrival · Lesson A

GROW Science · Autumn 2 · Week 3 · Lesson A · Supported

Name: ____________________

Four checks. Point, speak, sign, draw, write or direct an adult.

1. Focus

Which question is more focused: “space” or “What are Saturn’s rings made of?”

Help: Point, choose or say. Choose the one you can answer with a few facts.

2. Named source

Which is easier to check: a named NASA page or an anonymous message?

Help: Point, choose or say. Find an identifiable publisher.

3. Keep the unit

Jupiter’s day is about 10 ___. Choose hours or years.

Help: Point, choose or say. A day is one rotation.

4. Own words

What should stay when you paraphrase: the scientific meaning or the exact sentence?

Help: Point, choose or say. Keep meaning and source.

Evidence cards

GROW Science · Autumn 2 · Week 3 · Shared resource · Shared resource

Read a clue, choose a group, then explain. Cut apart or point; no cutting is required.

Named rings source

SAT-A links “mainly ice particles” to NASA’s Saturn facts.

Unit retained

JUP-A says about 10 hours for one rotation.

Unsourced life claim

“Red dust proves animals live on Mars” is not supported by these cards.

Old copied note

An undated note gives no source or unit; locate the original before using it.

Two rotation values

9.93 hours and about 10 hours agree after rounding.

Solid ring claim

The supplied sources describe particles, not one solid ring.

Answers · A · Standard

GROW Science · Autumn 2 · Week 3 · Lesson A · Standard

Four-question arrival

1. Focus: What are Saturn’s rings made of?

2. Named source: A named NASA page.

3. Keep the unit: Hours.

4. Own words: The scientific meaning, with a source code.

Two-check exit

1. Trace a fact: For example: Saturn’s rings are mainly ice particles, SAT-A / NASA.

2. Check agreement: Find the claim in a second suitable source, retaining units and any uncertainty.

Staff · feedback and access

GROW Science · Autumn 2 · Week 3 · Shared resource · Shared resource

Audience and response

The lesson teacher is the named adult audience. Hear or read the pupil’s own science response. A click, downloaded file or completed box is not evidence that a request was heard.

Respond within the existing task

Offer reading help, fewer cards at once, clearer labels, an adult-directed model or additional thinking time. Say what can and cannot change, then check whether the adjustment helped.

No additional pupil artefact

A response can be spoken, pointed, signed, drawn or written. Do not require a separate Lundy record, signature or written conversion of an oral response.

An optional pupil-owned note such as “What I said, and what it changed” may be used in existing work. It is not a requirement. If scribing, keep the pupil’s own words; the adult is an audience, not a verifier.

Keep assessment honest

Use current school recording practice and unit criteria separately. This pack does not certify an award. Do not infer a policy code from automated checking or a download.
